        "title": "ARC: connect successive row and column markers (general, v2)",
        "content": "For a grid with a uniform background and sparse marker cells, use the original input grid to identify markers and draw color 3 only in cells strictly between consecutive markers sharing a row or column. Preserve every original marker and every cell outside those gaps. Determine all spans from the original grid rather than newly drawn cells; where row and column spans cross, fill only eligible interior cells and never overwrite original markers. A lone marker in a row or column creates no span. This has been validated with background 1 and marker 0.",

      "arc_extend_first_patterned_row_to_the_right": {
        "id": "arc_extend_first_patterned_row_to_the_right",
        "kind": "memory",
        "title": "ARC: extend contiguous motif rows rightward",
        "content": "For ARC grids with a uniform background, inspect rows containing the non-background motif color. Extend a row only when its motif forms one contiguous, uninterrupted run and is followed immediately by background cells through the row's right edge: recolor only those trailing background cells with color 1. Leave rows with a motif fragmented by background gaps unchanged, even if their rightmost motif cell is followed by background. Do not alter fully filled rows or any other cells. Determine eligibility from the original input grid.",

      "arc_top_pattern_row_rightward_fill": {
        "id": "arc_top_pattern_row_rightward_fill",
        "kind": "memory",
        "title": "ARC: extend first patterned row to the right",
        "content": "In ARC grids with a uniform background and sparse structured motif rows, inspect the topmost motif row for a gap/continuation at its right edge. The output may mark with color 1 the non-motif cell(s) to the right of the motif on that row only, leaving other motif rows and the rest unchanged. Demonstrations: rows containing a 0/2 pattern had color 1 fill background from the pattern’s rightmost cell to the edge; in the solved test, a row of 8s ending in one background-5 cell had that edge cell changed to 1, while a later full 8 row was unchanged. Determine row and span from the motif; do not expand fill vertically based only on nearby row patterns.",

        "kind": "memory",
        "title": "ARC partial horizontal bar fill right",
        "content": "For ARC grids with a uniform background and horizontal bars of one color anchored at the left edge, preserve any full-width bar. For each partial bar, fill all remaining cells to its right edge with color 1. Leave other rows unchanged. Demonstrated with background 2 and color-6 bars, and validated on task-4a049439 with background 0 and color-4 bars.",

      "arc_color_1_trailing_background_marker_from_partial_motifs": {
        "id": "arc_color_1_trailing_background_marker_from_partial_motifs",
        "kind": "memory",
        "title": "ARC color-1 trailing-background marker from partial motifs",
        "content": "Observed in recurring ARC task family: uniform-background grids with sparse motif rows and color 1 as output marker. Demonstrations show 1 replacing background cells in a row suffix after a motif endpoint. In simple cases (e.g. a row begins with a partial foreground bar), replace background to its right with 1; more complex cases can have repeated motif blocks and selectively mark suffix/difference cells, so align corresponding motif rows/blocks before acting. Do not assume every row with trailing background qualifies: several demos changed only selected rows, and a test with two 4x22 motif blocks remained unresolved after multiple incorrect hypotheses. Preserve original foreground and untouched rows; inspect exact demo correspondences rather than applying blanket fill. Examples: demos showed 1 at suffix on rows with rightward continuation (including 0->1 or other background->1); recurrent colors vary.",

      "arc_separator_partition_extract_the_pre_divider_marker_pattern": {
        "id": "arc_separator_partition_extract_the_pre_divider_marker_pattern",
        "kind": "memory",
        "title": "ARC separator partition: extract the pre-divider marker pattern",
        "content": "Observed multiple demos with a uniform full-width horizontal divider or full-height vertical divider separating two noisy binary panels. Output crops the panel before the divider (above for horizontal, left for vertical), omits the divider and other panel, and changes cells of one sparse marker color to 3. Demonstration details: examples with upper-panel marker 4/5/1/0 converted to 3; the other cells in the crop take a background color that varied across examples (sometimes unchanged, sometimes the marker color, or another panel color). Do not assume a universal background recoloring rule from these examples. A test with horizontal divider, upper pattern colors 2 and 6, produced wrong submissions for 10x15 crop with 6->3 and backgrounds 2, 5, 6, 4, or 0, so there may be an additional background-selection/region rule not resolved. On future tasks, use all demonstrations to infer background mapping and verify output crop/orientation separately; avoid repeated blind palette guesses.",

      "arc_separated_panels_mark_cellwise_equal_values": {
        "id": "arc_separated_panels_mark_cellwise_equal_values",
        "kind": "memory",
        "title": "ARC separated-panel cellwise match marker",
        "content": "For ARC grids split into two equal-sized panels by a full uniform divider, compare corresponding cells in the two panels. Output a panel-sized grid, preserving the panel orientation and order. Mark positions where the values are equal with color 3; use the task’s common/background color at unequal positions. This applies to horizontal and vertical dividers. If equality markers blend with the default color in an example, use further demonstrations to disambiguate the rule. Validated on horizontal and vertical dividers, including a case where only one corresponding pair matched.",

      "arc_two_panel_overlap_of_background_cells": {
        "id": "arc_two_panel_overlap_of_background_cells",
        "kind": "memory",
        "title": "ARC two-panel overlap of background cells",
        "content": "For ARC grids with two equal panels separated by a uniform divider, inspect corresponding cells. Output has the dimensions of one panel. Mark with color 3 exactly the positions where BOTH panels contain their common background color; all other output cells use that common background color. Demos: 15x10 input with divider row 6, panels 7x10, background 9 and sparse 8/0 anomalies yielded output 3 where both cells were 9 and 9 elsewhere. A second demo had background 0, sparse 6/8 anomalies and yielded 3 where both cells were 0, 0 elsewhere. Use the original panels and align positions across divider; avoid confusing union of anomalies with the overlap-of-background rule.",

      "arc_equal_cell_matches_across_separated_panels_shared_color_fallback": {
        "id": "arc_equal_cell_matches_across_separated_panels_shared_color_fallback",
        "kind": "memory",
        "title": "ARC separated-panel matches: shared-color fallback and uncertainty",
        "content": "For ARC grids split by a uniform divider into equal-sized panels, use the demonstrations to determine the output panel and comparison rule; output is often panel-sized, but do not assume which panel is relevant when one panel is sparse or blank. In validated examples with the same sparse foreground marker in both panels, corresponding positions where both panels contain that marker are output as color 3, and other output cells use that marker color. This shared-color fallback is supported by demonstrations including task-28664599 demo pairs 2 and 6. Do not extrapolate this encoding to panels with different foreground colors: guessed defaults and overlap rules failed in task-28664599. If demonstrations do not establish the differing-color rule or panel relevance, request a demonstration before submitting.",

      "arc_periodic_patterns_from_sparse_markers": {
        "id": "arc_periodic_patterns_from_sparse_markers",
        "kind": "memory",
        "title": "ARC: infer periodic patterns from sparse row or diagonal markers",
        "content": "In ARC tasks, sparse markers may encode a periodic pattern that is expanded across the grid. Infer the pattern from demonstrations rather than assuming a fill rule. For diagonal cycles, compare cells by constant d=c−r; for row cycles, compare row indices. A demonstrated 3×3 case has input rows [4,0,0], [7,4,0], [5,7,4] and output rows [4,5,7], [7,4,5], [5,7,4]: the output repeats by diagonal class, with d=0→4, d=−1→7, and d=−2→5 (equivalently modulo 3). Other demonstrations show repeated row cycles and checker patterns. Before extrapolating, establish the period, phase, orientation, and how background cells are replaced from the examples. Do not infer a broad band, checkerboard, or period from only a few markers. A 27×27 test with diagonal 5/1 markers remained unsolved despite eight demos; its specific rule is uncertain and should not be asserted as established.",

      "arc_periodic_row_stripes_infer_smallest_compatible_period": {
        "id": "arc_periodic_row_stripes_infer_smallest_compatible_period",
        "kind": "memory",
        "title": "ARC periodic row stripes: infer period from stripe occurrences and align by row residue",
        "content": "For ARC grids with a uniform background and full-width constant-color horizontal stripes, use demonstrations to infer the vertical period. In the demonstrated task family, the period N is the number of observed non-background stripe-row occurrences; do not deduplicate occurrences just because some have the same color. Assign each observed stripe's color to its row-index residue modulo N, then fill every row across the full width using that N-row cycle. Preserve the phase implied by row indices rather than simply repeating stripe colors in their order of appearance. Examples: observed stripes at rows 2:9, 3:8, 11:2, 14:5, 20:3 imply residues 2:9, 3:8, 1:2, 4:5, 0:3 and cycle [3,2,9,8,5]; observed stripes at rows 0:5 and 5:6 imply a two-row alternating cycle [5,6]. For a test with stripes at rows 0:9, 1:7, 8:2, 27:2, 29:8, N=5 and the cycle is [9,7,2,2,8]. Check that every observed marker agrees with its residue before filling. If the demonstrations do not support this rule or imply conflicting residues, do not extrapolate blindly.",

      "arc_periodic_row_colors_with_zero_missing_entries": {
        "id": "arc_periodic_row_colors_with_zero_missing_entries",
        "kind": "memory",
        "title": "ARC periodic row colors with zero rows as missing entries",
        "content": "For ARC grids made of full-width uniform horizontal rows, zero-valued rows may be missing entries in a periodic sequence rather than background to preserve. Infer the smallest plausible period and phase that match every observed nonzero row color at its row index; verify all observations before filling any zeros. Then replace zero rows with the corresponding cycle color, preserving grid dimensions and full-width row format. Example: rows 1=4, 3=1, 4=4, 6=8, 8=5, and 11=5 (zero-based indices) are consistent with period 6 and cycle by residues [8,4,5,1,4,5]. Do not assume a period from a few matches if other observations contradict it; request more demonstrations when the sequence is underdetermined.",

      "arc_remove_isolated_noise_and_repair_rectangle_outliers": {
        "id": "arc_remove_isolated_noise_and_repair_rectangle_outliers",
        "kind": "memory",
        "title": "ARC remove isolated noise and repair rectangle outliers",
        "content": "For ARC grids with a uniform background, separated solid rectangular color regions, and scattered single-cell noise or corruption, preserve the grid dimensions and background; remove unsupported noise to the background and restore corrupted cells only when they lie inside a clearly supported intended rectangle. Demonstrations show that noise can be a different color from the background or match a region's color, and that different-color cells inside a rectangle may be corruption. Infer rectangle bounds from multiple intact rows and columns, clear boundaries, and recurring object geometry or dimensions across the grid—not merely from the bounding box of nearby same-color pixels. Do not extend a clean rectangle because of a lone adjoining cell, or complete an accidental cluster of speckles into an unsupported object. Treat isolated cells and short streaks as noise unless the rectangle's geometry is independently supported. Check every candidate object's exact bounds before producing the output.",
        "path": "general",

      "arc_repair_of_corrupted_rectangular_color_patches_amid_scattered_noise": {
        "id": "arc_repair_of_corrupted_rectangular_color_patches_amid_scattered_noise",
        "kind": "memory",
        "title": "ARC repair of corrupted rectangular color patches amid scattered noise",
        "content": "Observed ARC task family: a uniform background contains many separated solid rectangular patches in several colors, with scattered single-cell noise and occasional cells of another color replacing cells inside patches. Restore each clear rectangle to its original solid color; replace isolated noise in the background with the background color. Infer rectangle bounds only from coherent repeated rows/columns and preserve distinct neighboring rectangles, even when same-color patches are near each other. Do not extend a rectangle merely because a neighboring patch of the same color exists: verify its exact row/column extent from the grid. For example, one solved instance had multiple rectangle sizes/colors (including 3x2, 4x2, 4x4, 6x2, 6x3 and larger), outlier colors 1/7/8/9, and background 2. Several mistakes came from extending rectangles one row too far or combining separated components. Cross-check all four bounds per component and ensure output has exactly the input dimensions before submission. Demo examples confirm that sparse anomalous cells embedded in regular blocks should be repaired, while stray anomalies outside blocks are background.",

      "arc_continue_diagonal_color_rays": {
        "id": "arc_continue_diagonal_color_rays",
        "kind": "memory",
        "title": "ARC: continue established diagonal color rays",
        "content": "In ARC grids with a uniform background, matching-color cells may establish a diagonal ray. When at least two same-color cells align diagonally, infer the direction and continue that color one cell per row along the same diagonal until the grid boundary. Preserve existing cells and unrelated colors; extend only rays supported by the input pattern. Rays may have different colors and opposite diagonal directions.",

      "arc_selective_diagonal_ray_extension_uncertain_trigger": {
        "id": "arc_selective_diagonal_ray_extension_uncertain_trigger",
        "kind": "memory",
        "title": "ARC selective diagonal-ray extensions: require demo-validated triggers",
        "content": "For uniform-background ARC grids with sparse diagonal motifs, do not infer a ray extension from a same-color diagonal pair alone. Use all demonstrations—including unchanged controls—to determine which motif and color trigger an extension, its direction, and whether one or both ends continue. Demonstrated cases in this family include a diagonal 7 pair extended up-right, a diagonal 0 pair extended down-left, and 4 rays extended along their demonstrated diagonals; an orthogonal 4-pair control remained unchanged. These examples do not establish a universal color- or pair-based rule. Track existing colors, branches, obstacles, and both ray endpoints; preserve original cells and dimensions. Before submitting, check that the proposed transformation reproduces every extension and leaves every control unchanged. If multiple hypotheses remain consistent with the demonstrations, request another demonstration rather than guessing. In one test with 1 and 4 motifs, eight speculative outputs—including various 1/4 extensions and unchanged input—were all incorrect, underscoring that the trigger was not resolved by the available examples.",

      "arc_diagonal_ray_extend_aligned_pair_stop_obstacles": {
        "id": "arc_diagonal_ray_extend_aligned_pair_stop_obstacles",
        "kind": "memory",
        "title": "ARC extend diagonal rays from aligned color pairs",
        "content": "For ARC grids with a uniform background and same-color cells forming an adjacent diagonal pair, demonstrations may indicate a ray continuing in that diagonal direction. Extend the color along the demonstrated continuation toward the grid edge, preserving the pair and all unrelated cells. Infer the continuation direction from the pair's placement and demonstrations; do not assume both directions should be extended or extrapolate a ray without support. Stop at the grid boundary or at obstacles when the task examples establish that behavior. Before submitting, verify that the output has exactly the input height and width.",

      "arc_demonstrated_diagonal_ray_directions_and_controls": {
        "id": "arc_demonstrated_diagonal_ray_directions_and_controls",
        "kind": "memory",
        "title": "ARC diagonal rays: infer each extension direction from demonstrations",
        "content": "For ARC grids with sparse same-color diagonal alignments, use demonstrations to determine which alignments trigger extensions and the direction for each ray. Extend only through background in the supported outward direction, preserving all original cells and stopping before any occupied cell of another color. A demonstrated case extended 7 down-left from a pair at (r3,c4) and (r4,c3), 6 down-right from (r3,c5) and (r4,c6), and 9 up-left from (r1,c3) and (r2,c4), adding 9 at (r0,c2). Do not assume every diagonal pair extends, or extend both directions by default: compare changed examples with unchanged controls and validate each proposed ray against all demonstrations. Keep input dimensions unchanged.",

      "arc_diagonal_ray_extends_opposite_an_aligned_pair": {
        "id": "arc_diagonal_ray_extends_opposite_an_aligned_pair",
        "kind": "memory",
        "title": "ARC diagonal ray extends opposite an aligned pair",
        "content": "For a uniform-background ARC grid with a sparse motif containing two same-color cells on a diagonal, demos may show extending that color in the direction opposite the pair progression until the grid edge, preserving all other cells. Example: demo had color 7 at (row16,col12) and (row17,col11), output filled the same up-right diagonal (r11,c17 through r16,c12); existing cells remained unchanged. On test, color 9 at (r6,c2),(r7,c1) triggered 9s extended up-right through (r0,c8), while unrelated adjacent colors (5,3,4) stayed unchanged. Ensure boundaries and dimensions. A control demo with isolated adjacent pairs of other colors showed no change, so infer which diagonal pair/color is trigger from full examples rather than extending every pair.",

      "arc_input_and_rotations_in_four_quadrants": {
        "id": "arc_input_and_rotations_in_four_quadrants",
        "kind": "memory",
        "title": "ARC: arrange the input and its rotations in four quadrants",
        "content": "For ARC tasks demonstrated by a square input grid and an output twice its height and width, the output may be a 2×2 arrangement of the input and its rotations: top-left is unchanged; top-right is rotated 90° clockwise; bottom-left is rotated 90° counterclockwise; bottom-right is rotated 180°. For an n×n input A, compute rotations exactly: clockwise C[i][j]=A[n-1-j][i], counterclockwise L[i][j]=A[j][n-1-i], and half-turn H[i][j]=A[n-1-i][n-1-j]. Concatenate the corresponding quadrants without changing colors or dimensions. Check the quadrant placement and formulas rather than transposing or rotating manually. This rule is supported by demonstrations on 2×2 and 12×12 inputs.",

      "arc_doubled_grid_irregular_other_quadrants": {
        "id": "arc_doubled_grid_irregular_other_quadrants",
        "kind": "memory",
        "title": "ARC doubled grids with irregular non-input quadrants",
        "content": "In one demonstrated ARC task family, the output has exactly twice the input height and width, with the original input copied unchanged into the top-left quadrant. Across eight demos with input sizes 1×1, 7×7, 8×8, 10×10, 11×11, and 13×13, the other three quadrants contained dense, irregular values drawn from the input's palette. They did not follow a consistent tiling, reflection, or nearest-neighbor scaling rule. For similar tasks, verify the doubled dimensions and top-left copy, then compare candidate rules for the other quadrants against all demos. Do not assume repetition, symmetry, background fill, or arbitrary palette sampling without evidence; if the remaining cells have no inferable rule, recognize that the demos do not determine a reliable output rather than confidently guessing.",

      "arc_input_and_three_rotations_in_2x2_blocks": {
        "id": "arc_input_and_three_rotations_in_2x2_blocks",
        "kind": "memory",
        "title": "ARC: arrange the input and its three rotations in 2×2 blocks",
        "content": "For ARC tasks whose demonstrations show an output twice the input height and width, check whether it is a 2×2 block arrangement of the full input and its rotations. In the demonstrated 3×3 case, the top-left quadrant is the input unchanged, the top-right is rotated 90° clockwise, the bottom-left is rotated 90° counterclockwise, and the bottom-right is rotated 180°. Preserve each quadrant's full dimensions and verify every orientation against the demos before applying the rule. Do not infer this arrangement from doubled dimensions or a copied top-left quadrant alone: other doubled-grid task families may have unsupported or irregular contents in the remaining quadrants.",
